Community Monuments Fund (CMF)
The 2026 Community Monuments Fund (CMF) was announced 
by James Browne TD, Minister for Housing, Local Government 
and Heritage on the 8th December 2025.
The 2026 Community Monuments Fund will invest in our valuable 
archaeological heritage and help the owners and custodians of 
archaeological monuments to safeguard them into the future 
for the benefit of communities and the public. The total funding 
available nationally for projects under Community Monuments 
Fund 2026 will be €7.5 million. 
The core aims of the Community Monuments Fund are the 
conservation, maintenance, protection and presentation of 
archaeological monuments. It will:
•	
enable conservation works to be carried out on monuments 
which are deemed to be significant and in need of urgent 
support;
•	
build resilience in our monuments to enable them to 
withstand the effects of climate change;
•	
encourage access to monuments and improve their 
presentation.
The Community Monuments Fund has 3 Streams:
1.	
Stream 1 will offer grants up to €100,000 aimed at essential 
repairs and capital works for the conservation and repair of 
archaeological monuments.
2.	
Stream 2 will offer grants of up to €30,000 for development 
of Conservation Management Plans/Reports that are aimed 
at identifying measures for conservation of archaeological 
monuments and improving public access.
3.	
Stream 3 will offer grants of up to €30,000 for enhancement 
of access infrastructure and interpretation projects (including 
virtual/online) and small scale emergency conservations 
works at archaeological monuments.
The Community Monuments Fund provides funding for projects 
in relation to:
•	
Archaeological Monuments that are included in the Record 
of Monuments and Places (RMP) under the National 
Monuments Act 1930 (as amended)
•	
Archaeological Monuments that are identified in the 
Sites and Monuments Record compiled by the National 
Monuments Service.
Eligible projects will be drawn from the following categories:
•	
projects proposed by a Local Authority in relation to 
archaeological monuments in public ownership, where a 
clear heritage focus and community or public benefit has 
been demonstrated;
•	
projects proposed by a Local Authority on foot of applications 
from private applicants who are the owners or custodians 
of relevant archaeological monuments where there is a 
tangible public benefit;
•	
projects with a clearly defined heritage focus and community 
or public benefit proposed directly to the Department by a 
State-funded organisation working in the heritage area.
Further details about the 2026 Community Monuments Fund are 
available on the council’s website at https://www.clarecoco.ie/
services/planning/news/community-monuments-fund-2026.html 
The closing date for receipt of applications for the 2026 
Community Monuments Fund to the Council is Friday 30th 
January 2026.

The Shannon Estuary announced as the location 
for the Strategic Gas 
Emergency Reserve Ireland
Gas Networks Ireland has selected 
Cahiracon on the northern shore of the Shannon Estuary as 
the location for Ireland’s new Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve 
(SGER).
The Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve is a State-led project that 
will provide a temporary natural gas facility that can be used in 
the event of a disruption to Ireland’s gas supplies. 
The Government approved the delivery of the Strategic Gas 
Emergency Reserve in March, as it is critical for Ireland’s energy 
security while the State continues to transition to renewable 
energy. The new gas reserve will be delivered in the form of a 
Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU), which will be 
owned and operated on behalf of the State by Gas Networks 
Ireland.
Mock up of Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) to be 
located at Cahiracon (Source: GNI)
Initially, 14 possible coastal sites were considered as potential 
locations for the strategic gas emergency reserve. In recent 
months, Gas Networks Ireland’s team of engineers and 
consultants undertook detailed site assessments at locations in 
Cork Harbour and the Shannon Estuary.
Each site was evaluated against four specific criteria - 
technical, environmental, financial and planning. Following this 
comprehensive multi-criteria and cost-benefit analysis plus its 
associated pipe route corridor, the site at Cahiracon was deemed 
to best meet the project needs.
The multi-acre site in Cahiracon will be developed to include a 
deep-water jetty for a floating storage regasification unit (FRSU), 
an onshore facility, and a new connection to the national gas 
network.
The SIFP Steering Group will engage with representatives from 
GNI in the new year to discuss the project, what it means for 
the Shannon Estuary and how it can work with GNI to further 
develop the project. 
The site at Cahiracon is located within the Inishmurry/Cahiracon 
Strategic Development Location as identified within the Strategic 
Integrated Framework Plan for the Shannon Estuary for Marine 
Related Industry. Some of the key development considerations 
which led to the identification of this site were the 220kV lines 
which runs in close proximity to the site with local electricity 
supplied up to 35kV, the Galway to Limerick high-pressure 
Natural Gas pipeline (70 bar pressure), public water supply 
together with its proximity to Foynes Port. There is also the 
proximity to Cahiracon pier which provides a well sheltered 
lcoation at an existing pier offering direct access to a large pocket 
of well sheltered deep water and to the main navigation channel. 
Further, this site has policy support through its incorporation 
into the Clare County Development Plan 2023-2029 as Strategic 
Development Location A with a key objective to safeguard the 
roles and functions of the Strategic Development Location as 
identified through the SIFP. The SIFP Steering Group will form a 
key stakeholder as this project develops further over the coming 
months and years with Clare County Council acting as lead 
authority.
Ireland needs a temporary strategic gas emergency reserve 
because it currently imports 80% of its natural gas via two 
interconnectors from Britain. Any interruption to that supply 
would have a severe impact on electricity and heating to homes 
and businesses. Gas currently provides about 30% of Ireland’s 
primary energy needs and typically generates more than 40% 
of our electricity. At peak demand, gas can supply up to 80% of 
Ireland’s electricity generation.
The Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve will help mitigate this risk, 
as it will provide an alternative gas supply in the form of Liquefied 
Natural Gas (LNG). The Floating Storage and Regasification Unit 
(FRSU), which is central to the project, is a specialist ship that 
stores LNG at very low temperatures and then converts it to 
natural gas when required. 
This vessel will be docked at a jetty in Cahiracon and can deliver 
this natural gas to the existing gas network if required at any point. 
In the event of a major disruption to the current supply, the FRSU 
can be continuously re-supplied by sea until normal gas supplies 
are restored. FSRUs are a proven and safe technology which have 
been in use internationally for more than 20 years. There are 
currently more than 50 operating throughout the world. 
The selection of this site is a significant milestone for this project 
as Gas Networks Ireland will now progress with further scoping 
and designs, which will further refine costs estimates to inform 
the final investment decision. 
Natural gas is currently an essential back-up for intermittent 
renewable energy sources on our electricity system. When 
Ireland has progressed its transition to renewable energy sources 
and no longer faces a risk of disruption to gas supplies, the FSRU 
vessel can depart. The State-owned jetty and onshore facility at 
Cahiracon can then be repurposed for other uses in the future.

addressing the biodiversity crisis at a county wide level and strives 
to promote a whole-of-society approach in terms of protecting 
and conserving biodiversity. The plan provides a framework 
for biodiversity action over the next six years with the aim of

Publication of the NPWS Article 17 Reports: National 
Decline in Biodiversity 
The Status of EU Protected Habitats and Species in Ireland report 
or more commonly referred to as the ‘Article 17 reports’ have 
been published by the National Parks and Wildlife Service. The 
reports are carried out every six years and submitted to the 
European Commission to undertake surveillance of the condition 
of Annex I habitats and Annex II species located both inside and 
outside designated European Sites. The latest 2025 publication 
highlights alarming trends for biodiversity with 90% of habitats 
in 'Unfavourable' condition, 51% deteriorating, and only 9% 
improving, driven by pressures such as overgrazing, pollution, 
invasive species, drainage and development, highlighting 
a biodiversity crisis despite conservation efforts. The 9% of 
habitats improving is attributed to targeted conservation efforts 
and investment in nature conservation schemes. Full details of 
the reports can be viewed at the link: https://www.npws.ie/
publications/article-17-reports/article-17-reports-2025 
The Article 17 2025 publication highlights ongoing national declines 
in biodiversity.
Council Biodiversity Project: West Clare Chough 
Survey 2025 
The West Clare Coastal Chough Survey was carried out along a 
30km stretch of coastline extending from Kilkee to Loop Head 
Peninsula encompassing the breeding season of 2025. The 
project focused on the breeding distribution of coastal Chough, 
a species listed on Annex I of the EU Birds Directive and is 
supported by Clare County Council’s Biodiversity Officer and 
Tourism Department. Birdwatch Ireland were commissioned to 
undertake the survey. The findings reveal that 19 pairs of Chough 
were confirmed nesting along the coastline in 2025. Of these, 
16 pairs were successful, with 31 fledglings observed. All nests 
were located on natural sea cliffs, with none detected in nearby 
buildings. Chough is a species susceptible to pressures linked to 
changes in agricultural practices and human interference such 
as visitor numbers. The study serves as an important baseline to 
inform the distribution of Chough foraging and nest sites located 
along the coastline and to inform any future proposals and 
conservation management practices. 
Chough is a coastal cliff nesting bird of conservation concern in 
County Clare distinguished by its red bill and legs.
Council Biodiversity Project: Recording Irish Mayfly 
Project 2025
In 2025, The Biodiversity Officer Network across 27 local 
authorities including Clare County Council supported the 
National Mayfly Survey of Ireland 2024 and 2025. Mayflies are 
a common part of the invertebrate communities of most aquatic 
habitats in Ireland. Most mayfly species are useful as biological 
indicators of river health as they respond to environmental 
stressors associated with a deterioration in water quality. The 
IUCN conservation status of mayfly in Ireland was last assessed in 
2012. A total of 31 species have been detected during the course 
of the sampling, which represents 93% of the known species in 
Ireland. Six of the eight species with Red List status were recorded 
during the sampling. The project makes a substantial contribution 
to the knowledge of these species, with many detections outside 
of the previously known range of some species. Red listed species 
such as Labiobaetis atrebatinus have a rare distribution confined 
to a few counties including Clare.

Healthy Clare Launches 2026 Health and Wellbeing 
Calendar
Healthy Clare is delighted to announce the launch of the 2026 
Health and Wellbeing Calendar, a vibrant resource designed to 
inspire and support the people of County Clare in living healthier, 
happier lives throughout the year.
 This beautifully designed calendar features stunning images of 
Clare’s landscapes, celebrating the natural beauty that surrounds 
us. Each month includes key health and wellbeing dates, ensuring 
communities stay informed about national and local initiatives 
that promote physical and mental health.
Adding a unique cultural touch, the calendar showcases 
inspirational quotes in both Irish and English, encouraging 
positivity and mindfulness while embracing our heritage. 
Practicality is at its core, with essential contact details for local 
and national support services, making help and guidance easily 
accessible when needed.
The Healthy Clare Health and Wellbeing Calendar is more than 
just a date-keeper - it’s a daily reminder to prioritise wellbeing, 
connect with nature, and seek support when necessary. Whether 
you’re looking for motivation, information, or simply a beautiful 
addition to your home or workplace, this calendar is an invaluable 
tool for 2026.
Copies are available free of charge across Clare in libraries, and 
Clare County Council offices. 
Let’s make 2026 a year of health, happiness, and community 
connection. Together, we can build a healthier Clare!

UKRAINIAN SERVICES TEAM 
Recent CSO figures show there was a slight reduction in the 
number of Temporary Protections granted nationally in the 
past month, currently standing at 1,100 with an average 
of 38 granted per day. There are currently 3,032 Ukrainian 
Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTP’s) living in County 
Clare, this represents a reduction of 70 people compared to 
previous figures. There are 897 people accommodated in 18 
multi-occupancy facilities located throughout the County - this 
reflects a decrease of 8 people compared to previous figures. 
The remaining people are accommodated in residential settings, 
in formal hosted arrangements, through the Irish Red Cross and 
Clare County Council’s Offer-a-Home scheme and other private 
arrangements. To date our Matching & Relationship Manager has 
facilitated the accommodation of 458 people that were originally 
living in hotel and multi-occupancy facilities. 
The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration has 
introduced changes to their accommodation policy effective from 
10th November 2025 for those newly arriving in the Country. 
Under the revised approach, anyone fleeing the war in Ukraine, 
who registers for temporary protection and is looking for State-
provided accommodation in Ireland will be accommodated for a 
maximum of 30 days (previously 90 days). They will be provided 
with food, laundry and other services and supports in the 
Designated Accommodation Centres.
The revised approach to the accommodation offering has been 
adopted in order to respond to a recent large increase in the 
number of arrivals from Ukraine. This policy aims to ensure the 
State can continue to provide temporary accommodation to 
those most in need when they arrive.
This change will not affect people who have already commenced 
their stay under the 90-day Accommodation Policy, or those 
already availing of other State-supported accommodation.
LOCAL AUTHORITY INTEGRATION 
TEAM 
The Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) have been set up 
in all local authorities. Their purpose is to help coordinate the 
different kinds of support available for people who are applying 
for international protection, refugees, and others in similar 
situations. 
The goal of LAITs is to help IP applicants and refugees become 
independent, settle into their new communities, and participate 
in Irish life. They do this by connecting people to important 
services that can help them integrate into the community. 
Who do LAITs support? 
LAITs provide support for: 
•	
Applicants for International Protection (IP) 
•	
People who have been granted refugee status or other forms 
of protection, such as subsidiary protection or permission to 
remain 
•	
Refugees who have been resettled in Ireland through a 
government programme 
•	
Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs) 
How is the support provided? 
LAITs operate under the principle of 'Integration from Day One'. 
This means that LAITs provide integration support to people who 
need it as soon as they arrive in Ireland.

 What services do LAITs provide?

LAITs help connect people with the existing services that are most 
suitable for their needs. This includes things like: 
•	
Being a direct contact for new arrivals, helping them with any 
problems they might have when dealing with public services 
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services like legal help, 
childcare and healthcare 
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services that improve their 
ability to live independently, like job training, English classes, 
education, and apprenticeships 
•	
Guiding new arrivals through the process of applying for 
financial support, medical help, child benefits, and other 
services they might need 
•	
Holding meetings in local areas and using community 
development principles to help those who attend 
•	
Supporting people if they face racism or other unfair 
treatment, helping them report it to the right authorities 
•	
Helping vulnerable new arrivals get in touch with non-
governmental organisations (NGOs) and other services if 
they need extra help

This unit operates within the Housing Delivery, Infrastructure 
Provision and Land Activation Directorate and the key objective 
across all the elements of the unit is to bring together our 
resources with a strong ambition for delivery of increased 
activity on lands and activation of vacant and derelict properties 
throughout the County.
Working collaboratively across the other units in the Directorate 
with pooled resources and knowledge, it is intended to increase 
levels of activity and engagement to activate more properties for 
delivery of housing, both public and private.
Work towards ending dereliction and vacancy is a priority in the 
National Housing Plan 2025, with the re-use and regeneration 
of vacant and derelict properties in cities, towns and villages 
providing much needed housing and transforming and revitalizing 
communities, as summarised hereunder.
DERELICT SITES
A significant effort to transform the many derelict properties 
across the County is underway with 306 derelict properties 
being dealt with under the Derelict Sites Act 1990 as of the 16th 
December 2025. A further 20 properties have been identified for 
action in the last month. The team maintains very high levels of 
activity and engagement with owners and their legal/technical 
representatives. This initial engagement is key to resolution of 
the issues of dereliction and to gain an understanding of the 
various reasons why the properties are in a derelict state. Where 
derelict properties are sold by the owner, the Derelict Sites Team 
engages promptly with the new owners to brief them on their 
responsibilities under the Derelict Sites Act, 1990. 
To bolster the momentum, the Council is advising property 
owners on accessing the vacant property refurbishment grant. 
The Team is also seeing a consistent number of planning 
applications for property refurbishment/extensions, and it is 
clear from driving around the county the level of work ongoing 
on individual properties. The Derelict Sites Team believe that by 
working in partnership with owners and financial institutions, 
there are real opportunities for the positive revitalisation and re-
development of many properties. 
Working collaboratively to tackle dereliction

to carry out works that to a property if deemed necessary. A word 
of thanks to our Shannon MD colleagues for their assistance with
